 Mail-in voting preferred amongst Sun Devils and Arizona voters during midterm election
 Early voting appeals to convenience and flexibility for busy schedules
 "The Active Early Voting List allows an eligible Arizona voter to automatically receive a ballot by mail for every election 27 days prior, according to its website." Illustrated by:
 Kyra Saley 
 By Ariana Hernandez 
 |
 November 10, 2026 | 7:16pm MST 
 Arizona voters and Sun Devils preferred mail-in voting during this midterm election for convenience and flexibility when casting a ballot.
 Arizona Clean Elections reported that about 80% of Arizona voters chose to vote by mail in 2024. Maricopa County reported an early voter turnout of over 1.2 million ballots on Nov. 9, 2026.
 According to NBC News , over 1.8 million mail-in and early ballots were cast as of Nov. 9. This is already a nearly 200,000 increase from the 2022 midterm election.
 In 1997, the Arizona legislature allowed voters to request an early ballot, and in 2007 county recorders in Arizona advocated for the creation of the Permanent Early Voting List, now known as the Active Early Voting List .
 The Active Early Voting List allows an eligible Arizona voter to automatically receive a ballot by mail for every election 27 days prior, according to its website.
 Bill Gates, director of the Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory at Arizona State University , said early ballots, including mail-in ballots and voting before Election Day, are appealing to residents because of convenience.
 Gates said Maricopa County specifically has long ballots, causing people to appreciate the ability to research and fill out their ballots at home rather than at the polls on Election Day.
 "We could do it on our schedule as opposed to, if I don't get there on Election Day, I'm not going to get to vote." Gates said, "What if there's a 90-minute line and I don't have time?"
 Gates said that when he was on the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors, their goal was for people to have choices. He said this rise in early voting is encouraging, especially after President Donald Trump raised doubts about voting.
 In March, Trump signed an executive order directing the United States Postal Service to build a system for blocking delivery of ballots to voters not on lists pre-submitted by state officials, according to PBS NewsHour .  
 View this post on Instagram 
 A post shared by Maricopa County Elections (@maricopavote) 
 "Despite some of that negativity about mail-in voting and negativity about the postal service, to see that they're still doing these mail-in votes and even maybe doing more… I think that’s great news," Gates said.
 Alisha Usman and Aisha Aliniazee are two Arizona voters and University students who voted early.
 Aliniazee, a sophomore studying applied biological sciences on the pre-dental track, mailed her ballot in and said it's convenient for her schedule as a full-time college student with two jobs.
 Usman, a junior studying political science and justice studies, dropped her ballot off at the ballot box and said it's easier for her to have her research next to her while she fills out her ballot.
 "When you have that ballot in your own house, it's a lot easier to be able to do all that research," Usman said.
 Usman said one of the appeals of early voting is not having to wait in line on Election Day. Aliniazee said not having to take time off from work to go to the polls adds to the popularity.
 "It's a lot harder for them to actually physically go to the polls as well, so I think just having that mail-in is really convenient for them," Aliniazee said.
 In future elections, Usman and Aliniazee said they plan to continue participating in early voting, and neither had concerns about their ballots not being counted or received.
 "There's just so many more benefits with mail-in voting as well that people should know about," Aliniazee said.
 Edited by Andi Ruiz, Alan Deutschendorf III and Katarina Sanchez.
